title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Back to Sacramento
On Monday we fit price ~ sqft on the Sacramento house sales. Let’s add type, a categorical variable, so we can see how to read both kinds of variables.

Sacramento |>
  count(type)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  type             n
  <fct>        <int>
1 Condo           53
2 Multi_Family    13
3 Residential    866

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Dummy variables

A regression needs numbers, so R turns a categorical variable (a factor) into dummy variables, also called indicator variables
Each dummy variable is a 0/1 column for one level, and there’s one for every level except the first
The level without a column is the reference level, and every other level gets compared with it

title: Interpreting a linear regression
section: Two names for the same idea
text:
Two names for the same idea

Statistics calls this dummy variable encoding
Computer science and machine learning call it one-hot encoding
Both turn each level of a categorical variable into a 0/1 column
One-hot encoding usually keeps a column for every level, while a regression with an intercept drops one, the reference level (R does this for us)

text:
type as dummy variables
type has 3 levels, so it becomes 2 dummy variables, with Condo as the reference:

Fit the model

  fit(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento)

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Interpreting a continuous variable

For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect [outcome] to increase (or decrease) by [estimate] [units], all else remaining the same.

For sqft:

For every 1 square foot increase in size, we expect the sale price to increase by $139, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $131 to $146).


“All else remaining the same” means the other variables in the model, so here, a house of the same type

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Interpreting a categorical variable

We expect [outcome] for [level] to be [estimate] [units] higher (or lower) than for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For typeMulti_Family:

We expect multi-family homes to sell for $66,224 less than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $14,762 to $117,686 less).


Here “all else” is the size: a multi-family home and a condo with the same square footage
The comparison is always with the reference level, Condo

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
When the interval includes 0
For typeResidential:

We expect residential homes to sell for $8,253 more than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: -$15,594 to $32,100).


The interval includes 0, so the data don’t show a clear difference between residential homes and condos of the same size
We still report the estimate and its interval, and say that it’s unclear

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
The intercept

The intercept is the expected outcome when every continuous variable is 0 and every categorical variable is at its reference level
Here that’s a condo with 0 square feet, which doesn’t exist, so we don’t interpret it

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
A sore throat after surgery
licorice_gargle (from medicaldata) is a trial of 235 adults having thoracic surgery with a large breathing tube. Before the tube went in, they were randomized to gargle licorice or sugar water. Our outcome is any sore throat 30 minutes after surgery.

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Recode the variables

sore <- licorice_gargle |>
  mutate(
    sore_throat = factor(pacu30min_throatPain > 0,
                         levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("no", "yes")),
    treatment = factor(treat, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("sugar", "licorice")),
    smoking = factor(preOp_smoking, levels = c(3, 2, 1),
                     labels = c("never", "past",
                                "current"))
  ) |>
  select(sore_throat, treatment,
         bmi = preOp_calcBMI, smoking) |>
  drop_na()

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Which level are we modelling?

logistic_reg() models the odds of the outcome’s second level
sore_throat has the levels no, then yes, so every result is about the odds of a sore throat
The predictors are a mix of both kinds:

treatment: 2 levels, so 1 dummy variable (reference sugar)
bmi: continuous, in kg/m²
smoking: 3 levels, so 2 dummy variables (reference never)



count(sore, sore_throat)

  sore_throat   n
1          no 169
2         yes  64

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Fit the model

sore_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
      data = sore)

tidy(sore_fit, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         0.0240    0.979     0.0245 0.980      -1.91     1.95  
2 treatmentlicorice  -0.956     0.316    -3.02   0.00252    -1.59    -0.346 
3 bmi                -0.0517    0.0385   -1.34   0.179      -0.129    0.0229
4 smokingpast         1.48      0.428     3.45   0.000551    0.664    2.35  
5 smokingcurrent      0.635     0.410     1.55   0.121      -0.152    1.46  



These estimates are on the log-odds scale, \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right)\), which is hard to read

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Exponentiate to get odds ratios

sore_or <- sore_fit |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
sore_or

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02 
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02 
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5  
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33 



exponentiate = TRUE turns each estimate and its interval into an odds ratio (std.error, statistic, and p.value stay on the log-odds scale)
An odds ratio of 1 means no difference, below 1 means lower odds, and above 1 means higher odds

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Interpreting a continuous variable

For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect the odds of [outcome] to be multiplied by [odds ratio], all else remaining the same.

For bmi:

For every 1 kg/m² increase in BMI, we expect the odds of a sore throat to be multiplied by 0.95, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.88 to 1.02).


Multiplied by 0.95 is the same as 5% lower odds
The interval includes 1, so the data don’t show a clear effect of BMI

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Interpreting a categorical variable

We expect the odds of [outcome] for [level] to be [odds ratio] times the odds for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For treatmentlicorice:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for patients who gargled licorice to be 0.38 times the odds for patients who gargled sugar water, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.71).


That’s 62% lower odds, and the interval doesn’t include 1

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
section: A categorical variable with more levels
text:
A categorical variable with more levels
Each dummy variable compares one level with the reference, never. For smokingpast:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for past smokers to be 4.38 times the odds for people who never smoked, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 1.94 to 10.48).


smokingcurrent compares current smokers with people who never smoked, not with past smokers
Its interval (0.86 to 4.33) includes 1, so that comparison isn’t clear

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Odds, not probability

An odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities
Say “0.38 times the odds”, not “0.38 times as likely” or “62% less likely”
The two are close only when the outcome is rare, and here 27% of patients had a sore throat

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
section: The same model in base R
text:
The same model in base R
Base R’s glm() fits the same model with less code:

glm(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
    family = binomial, data = sore) |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

The same odds ratios and intervals as logistic_reg()
We use tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps

Logistic regression models the log-odds of the event:
\[
\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \dots
\]
where \(p\) is the probability of recurrence. Exponentiating a coefficient, \(e^{\beta}\), gives an odds ratio.

title: Observational units
text:
The original third rule
The original definition from the 2014 Tidy Data paper is:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you’re observing, for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit. The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.

title: Observational units
section: Problem 5: one unit in many tables
text:
Problem 5: one unit in many tables
The opposite problem is one kind of observation split across many files, such as one file per year or one per hospital site. If the files have the same columns, we can stack them with bind_rows() or give read_csv() all the file names at once.

title: Observational units
text:
How hospitals store data
Hospital databases follow the paper’s third rule, with one table per kind of observational unit, linked by ID columns.

patients has one row per patient
encounters has one row per visit, with the patient’s ID
conditions, medications, and observations have one row per record, with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.
Synthea creates fake but realistic patient records stored this way. Its downloads page has samples of 100 patients in CSV, HL7 FHIR, and C-CDA formats.

title: Observational units
text:
Beyond CSVs: health data standards
In practice, health data is usually stored and shared using data standards, not as a folder of CSV files.

HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is HL7’s newer standard, which sends a patient, an encounter, or an observation as a “resource” through web APIs
The OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community, is a shared database layout for observational health data, so the same analysis code can run on many hospitals’ databases

All of these follow the third rule, with one table (or resource) per kind of observational unit, linked by IDs.

Standards: HL7, FHIR, OHDSI and its OMOP Common Data Model.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Visualization: ask a question, then answer it
text:
Visualization: ask a question, then answer it

When we make a plot, we’re trying to answer a question about our data, and a good plot answers it clearly.


Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
ggplot2: three parts
Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same parts:

Aesthetic mappings, which map columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill)
Geometric objects (geoms), which say how to draw them (geom_point(), geom_histogram(), geom_bar())
Scales and labels for the axes, colours, and titles

We add each layer with +.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Scatter plot: two quantitative variables
Is a penguin’s body mass related to its flipper length?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Add colour and labels

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Histogram: one quantitative variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable
text:
Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Rules of thumb

Answer one question per plot
Label axes, with units
Use colourblind-friendly palettes
Avoid pie charts, 3D, and tables of numbers when a plot will do

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Visualization: ask a question, then answer it
text:
Visualization: ask a question, then answer it

When we make a plot, we’re trying to answer a question about our data, and a good plot answers it clearly.


Artwork by Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
ggplot2: three parts
Every ggplot2 plot is built from the same parts:

Aesthetic mappings, which map columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill)
Geometric objects (geoms), which say how to draw them (geom_point(), geom_histogram(), geom_bar())
Scales and labels for the axes, colours, and titles

We add each layer with +.

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Scatter plot: two quantitative variables
Is a penguin’s body mass related to its flipper length?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Add colour and labels

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Histogram: one quantitative variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 250, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
section: Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable
text:
Bar plot: counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "Number of penguins", fill = "Species")

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Rules of thumb

Answer one question per plot
Label axes, with units
Use colourblind-friendly palettes
Avoid pie charts, 3D, and tables of numbers when a plot will do

title: Wrangling and visualizing
text:
Data and credits

penguins: R’s datasets::penguins (R 4.5 or newer), Horst, Hill, and Gorman’s Palmer penguins
Adapted from chapters 3 and 4 of Data Science: A First Introduction (Timbers, Campbell, and Lee; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

Packages

title: Tidy data
text:
What is tidy data?


Each variable is a column; each column is a variable
Each observation is a row; each row is an observation
Each value is a cell; each cell is a single value



Rules from R for Data Science (2e), chapter 5. Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst, from the Openscapes blog (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
The original definition (2014)
The Tidy Data paper defines it a little differently:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

The third rule is really about databases, where data is split into separate tables and joined back together. The newer definition replaces it with “each value is a cell”. We’ll come back to observational units in Lecture 2’s Observational units section.

title: Tidy data
text:
Why bother?

Once our data is tidy, we can use the same tools every time we summarize, plot, or model it.


Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
Five ways data gets messy
From the Tidy Data paper:

Column headers are values, not variable names
Multiple variables are stored in one column
Variables are stored in both rows and columns
Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table
A single observational unit is stored in multiple tables

We’ll go through the first three using the datasets from the paper. Problems 4 and 5 are about observational units, which we’ll cover in Lecture 2’s Observational units section.

section: Problem 2: multiple variables in one column
text:
Problem 2: multiple variables in one column

title: From tidy data to models

Packages

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Two kinds of questions
When we want to predict something, the type of outcome tells us what kind of model to use.

Regression, when the outcome is quantitative. What will this house sell for? How heavy will this baby be at birth?
Classification, when the outcome is categorical. Will this patient’s cancer come back, yes or no?

Today we’ll fit a linear regression. On Wednesday we’ll fit linear and logistic regressions on medical data.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Models need tidy data
A model formula like price ~ sqft expects the data to have one row per observation (each house sale) and one column per variable (the price and the size), which is what tidy data gives us.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Is size related to price?

ggplot(Sacramento, aes(x = sqft, y = price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "House size (square feet)", y = "Sale price (USD)")

title: From tidy data to models
section: Linear regression: the line of best fit
text:
Linear regression: the line of best fit
\[
\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{sqft}
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, where the line crosses the y axis
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, how much the price changes for each extra square foot

The “best” line is the one with the smallest squared vertical distances between the line and the data points.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Fit it with tidymodels

house_recipe <- recipe(price ~ sqft, data = Sacramento)

house_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

house_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(house_recipe) |>
  add_model(house_spec) |>
  fit(data = Sacramento)
house_fit

More than one predictor
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_m X_m
\]
To use more predictors, we add them to the formula.

recipe(price ~ sqft + beds + baths, data = Sacramento)

outcome:   1

Now each slope is how much the outcome changes for one predictor, when the other predictors stay the same.

title: Tidy data
text:
What is tidy data?


Each variable is a column; each column is a variable
Each observation is a row; each row is an observation
Each value is a cell; each cell is a single value



Rules from R for Data Science (2e), chapter 5. Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst, from the Openscapes blog (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
The original definition (2014)
The Tidy Data paper defines it a little differently:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

The third rule is really about databases, where data is split into separate tables and joined back together. The newer definition replaces it with “each value is a cell”. We’ll come back to observational units in Lecture 2’s Observational units section.

title: Tidy data
text:
Why bother?

Once our data is tidy, we can use the same tools every time we summarize, plot, or model it.


Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).

title: Tidy data
text:
Five ways data gets messy
From the Tidy Data paper:

Column headers are values, not variable names
Multiple variables are stored in one column
Variables are stored in both rows and columns
Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table
A single observational unit is stored in multiple tables

We’ll go through the first three using the datasets from the paper. Problems 4 and 5 are about observational units, which we’ll cover in Lecture 2’s Observational units section.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Two kinds of questions
When we want to predict something, the type of outcome tells us what kind of model to use.

Regression, when the outcome is quantitative. What will this house sell for? How heavy will this baby be at birth?
Classification, when the outcome is categorical. Will this patient’s cancer come back, yes or no?

Today we’ll fit a linear regression. On Wednesday we’ll fit linear and logistic regressions on medical data.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Models need tidy data
A model formula like price ~ sqft expects the data to have one row per observation (each house sale) and one column per variable (the price and the size), which is what tidy data gives us.

title: From tidy data to models
section: Linear regression: the line of best fit
text:
Linear regression: the line of best fit
\[
\text{price} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{sqft}
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, where the line crosses the y axis
\(\beta_1\) is the slope, how much the price changes for each extra square foot

The “best” line is the one with the smallest squared vertical distances between the line and the data points.

title: From tidy data to models
text:
Fit it with tidymodels

house_recipe <- recipe(price ~ sqft, data = Sacramento)

house_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

house_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(house_recipe) |>
  add_model(house_spec) |>
  fit(data = Sacramento)
house_fit

title: From tidy data to models
text:
More than one predictor
\[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_m X_m
\]
To use more predictors, we add them to the formula.

recipe(price ~ sqft + beds + baths, data = Sacramento)

Now each slope is how much the outcome changes for one predictor, when the other predictors stay the same.

title: Cleaning and tidying medical data
text:
Before we can model data, it has to be “tidy” and “clean”: one row per observation, one column per variable, and values coded the way we’ll analyze them. In class, we’ll reshape data into a tidy shape, then recode numbers into categories we can read. For more practice, see Extra practice: cleaning and tidying.
library(tidyverse)
library(medicaldata)

title: Cleaning and tidying medical data
section: Exercise 1: Gum health over the trial’s visits
text:
Exercise 1: Gum health over the trial’s visits
opt (from medicaldata) is the Obstetrics and Periodontal Therapy trial, which randomized pregnant women with periodontal disease to periodontal treatment (T) or control (C) (Michalowicz et al., 2006). Their gums were examined at baseline (BL), visit 3 (V3), and visit 5 (V5). We’ll look at two of the measures:

GE, the gingival index, where higher means more inflamed gums
PD.avg, the average pocket depth in millimetres

Every dataset in medicaldata is a base R data frame, not a tibble, so printing one prints every row. We’ll use head() to print just the first 6.

gums <- opt |>
  select(PID, Group, BL.GE, BL.PD.avg, V3.GE, V3.PD.avg, V5.GE, V5.PD.avg)
head(gums)

     PID Group BL.GE BL.PD.avg V3.GE V3.PD.avg V5.GE V5.PD.avg
1 100034     C 1.429     2.696 1.637     3.000 2.077     2.929
2 100042     C 1.298     2.685    NA        NA    NA        NA
3 100067     T 1.784     2.821    NA        NA    NA        NA

5 100091     C 1.173     2.768 1.762     2.744 1.845     2.786
6 100109     T 0.969     2.932    NA        NA    NA        NA








NoteYour turn



A header like V3.PD.avg packs two variables into one name: the visit (V3) and the measure (PD.avg). PD.avg has a dot of its own, so names_sep = "." would split it in the wrong place. The names_pattern below reads “the visit, a dot, then the rest”.

Pivot the six measure columns into visit, measure, and value, dropping missing values.
Pivot measure back out, so GE and PD.avg are their own columns. Call the result gums_tidy.
Calculate the mean pocket depth and gingival index for each group at each visit. What happened to the treatment group’s gums?
Plot the mean pocket depth at each visit, coloured by group.


gums_tidy <- gums |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ____,
    names_to = c(____, ____),
    names_pattern = "(BL|V3|V5)\\.(.*)",
    values_to = "value",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = ____, values_from = ____)

gums_summary <- gums_tidy |>
  group_by(____, ____) |>
  summarize(
    avg_pd = mean(PD.avg, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_ge = mean(GE, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ggplot(gums_summary, aes(x = visit, y = ____, colour = ____, group = ____)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Back to Sacramento
On Monday we fit price ~ sqft on the Sacramento house sales. Let’s add type, a categorical variable, so we can see how to read both kinds of variables.

Sacramento |>
  count(type)

# A tibble: 3 × 2

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Dummy variables

A regression needs numbers, so R turns a categorical variable (a factor) into dummy variables, also called indicator variables
Each dummy variable is a 0/1 column for one level, and there’s one for every level except the first
The level without a column is the reference level, and every other level gets compared with it

title: Interpreting a linear regression
section: Two names for the same idea
text:
Two names for the same idea

Statistics calls this dummy variable encoding
Computer science and machine learning call it one-hot encoding
Both turn each level of a categorical variable into a 0/1 column
One-hot encoding usually keeps a column for every level, while a regression with an intercept drops one, the reference level (R does this for us)

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
type as dummy variables
type has 3 levels, so it becomes 2 dummy variables, with Condo as the reference:



type
typeMulti_Family
typeResidential




Condo

1

text:
Fit the model

house_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento)

house_tidy <- tidy(house_fit, conf.int = TRUE)
house_tidy

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  term             estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>               <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         6885.  12169.       0.566 5.72e-  1  -16996.    30766.

One row for sqft
One row for each dummy variable, and no row for Condo, the reference level

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Interpreting a continuous variable

For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect [outcome] to increase (or decrease) by [estimate] [units], all else remaining the same.

For sqft:

For every 1 square foot increase in size, we expect the sale price to increase by $139, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $131 to $146).


“All else remaining the same” means the other variables in the model, so here, a house of the same type

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
Interpreting a categorical variable

We expect [outcome] for [level] to be [estimate] [units] higher (or lower) than for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For typeMulti_Family:

We expect multi-family homes to sell for $66,224 less than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: $14,762 to $117,686 less).


Here “all else” is the size: a multi-family home and a condo with the same square footage
The comparison is always with the reference level, Condo

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
When the interval includes 0
For typeResidential:

We expect residential homes to sell for $8,253 more than condos, all else remaining the same (95% CI: -$15,594 to $32,100).


The interval includes 0, so the data don’t show a clear difference between residential homes and condos of the same size
We still report the estimate and its interval, and say that it’s unclear

title: Interpreting a linear regression
text:
The intercept

The intercept is the expected outcome when every continuous variable is 0 and every categorical variable is at its reference level
Here that’s a condo with 0 square feet, which doesn’t exist, so we don’t interpret it

title: Observational units
text:
The original third rule
The original definition from the 2014 Tidy Data paper is:

Each variable forms a column
Each observation forms a row
Each type of observational unit forms a table

An observational unit is the kind of thing you’re observing, for example a song, a patient, or a hospital visit. The third rule says different kinds of things belong in different tables.

  mutate(date = date.entered + (week - 1) * 7) |>
  arrange(artist, track, week) |>

title: Observational units
section: Problem 5: one unit in many tables
text:
Problem 5: one unit in many tables
The opposite problem is one kind of observation split across many files, such as one file per year or one per hospital site. If the files have the same columns, we can stack them with bind_rows() or give read_csv() all the file names at once.

title: Observational units
text:
How hospitals store data
Hospital databases follow the paper’s third rule, with one table per kind of observational unit, linked by ID columns.

patients has one row per patient
encounters has one row per visit, with the patient’s ID
conditions, medications, and observations have one row per record, with the patient and encounter IDs

To analyze the data, we join the tables we need into one tidy table.
Synthea creates fake but realistic patient records stored this way. Its downloads page has samples of 100 patients in CSV, HL7 FHIR, and C-CDA formats.

title: Observational units
text:
Beyond CSVs: health data standards
In practice, health data is usually stored and shared using data standards, not as a folder of CSV files.

HL7 is the family of standards hospital systems use to exchange clinical data
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is HL7’s newer standard, which sends a patient, an encounter, or an observation as a “resource” through web APIs
The OMOP Common Data Model, from the OHDSI community, is a shared database layout for observational health data, so the same analysis code can run on many hospitals’ databases

All of these follow the third rule, with one table (or resource) per kind of observational unit, linked by IDs.

title: Observational units
text:
Data and credits

billboard.csv: the tidy data paper’s Billboard example, via chendaniely/pandas_for_everyone and hadley/tidy-data
Wickham, H. (2014). Tidy Data. Journal of Statistical Software, 59(10). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v059.i10 (PDF: https://vita.had.co.nz/papers/tidy-data.pdf)
Synthea synthetic patient records: https://synthetichealth.github.io/synthea/
Standards: HL7, FHIR, OHDSI and its OMOP Common Data Model.

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
A sore throat after surgery
licorice_gargle (from medicaldata) is a trial of 235 adults having thoracic surgery with a large breathing tube. Before the tube went in, they were randomized to gargle licorice or sugar water. Our outcome is any sore throat 30 minutes after surgery.

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Recode the variables

sore <- licorice_gargle |>
  mutate(
    sore_throat = factor(pacu30min_throatPain > 0,
                         levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels = c("no", "yes")),
    treatment = factor(treat, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("sugar", "licorice")),
    smoking = factor(preOp_smoking, levels = c(3, 2, 1),
                     labels = c("never", "past",
                                "current"))
  ) |>
  select(sore_throat, treatment,
         bmi = preOp_calcBMI, smoking) |>
  drop_na()

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Which level are we modelling?

logistic_reg() models the odds of the outcome’s second level
sore_throat has the levels no, then yes, so every result is about the odds of a sore throat
The predictors are a mix of both kinds:

treatment: 2 levels, so 1 dummy variable (reference sugar)
bmi: continuous, in kg/m²
smoking: 3 levels, so 2 dummy variables (reference never)



count(sore, sore_throat)

  sore_throat   n
1          no 169
2         yes  64

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Fit the model

sore_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
      data = sore)

tidy(sore_fit, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)         0.0240    0.979     0.0245 0.980      -1.91     1.95  
2 treatmentlicorice  -0.956     0.316    -3.02   0.00252    -1.59    -0.346 
3 bmi                -0.0517    0.0385   -1.34   0.179      -0.129    0.0229
4 smokingpast         1.48      0.428     3.45   0.000551    0.664    2.35  
5 smokingcurrent      0.635     0.410     1.55   0.121      -0.152    1.46  



These estimates are on the log-odds scale, \(\log\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right)\), which is hard to read

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Exponentiate to get odds ratios

sore_or <- sore_fit |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
sore_or

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02 
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02 
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5  
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33 



exponentiate = TRUE turns each estimate and its interval into an odds ratio (std.error, statistic, and p.value stay on the log-odds scale)
An odds ratio of 1 means no difference, below 1 means lower odds, and above 1 means higher odds

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Interpreting a continuous variable

For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable], we expect the odds of [outcome] to be multiplied by [odds ratio], all else remaining the same.

For bmi:

For every 1 kg/m² increase in BMI, we expect the odds of a sore throat to be multiplied by 0.95, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.88 to 1.02).


Multiplied by 0.95 is the same as 5% lower odds
The interval includes 1, so the data don’t show a clear effect of BMI

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Interpreting a categorical variable

We expect the odds of [outcome] for [level] to be [odds ratio] times the odds for [reference level], all else remaining the same.

For treatmentlicorice:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for patients who gargled licorice to be 0.38 times the odds for patients who gargled sugar water, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.71).


That’s 62% lower odds, and the interval doesn’t include 1

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
section: A categorical variable with more levels
text:
A categorical variable with more levels
Each dummy variable compares one level with the reference, never. For smokingpast:

We expect the odds of a sore throat for past smokers to be 4.38 times the odds for people who never smoked, all else remaining the same (95% CI: 1.94 to 10.48).


smokingcurrent compares current smokers with people who never smoked, not with past smokers
Its interval (0.86 to 4.33) includes 1, so that comparison isn’t clear

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
text:
Odds, not probability

An odds ratio compares odds, not probabilities
Say “0.38 times the odds”, not “0.38 times as likely” or “62% less likely”
The two are close only when the outcome is rare, and here 27% of patients had a sore throat

title: Interpreting a logistic regression
section: The same model in base R
text:
The same model in base R
Base R’s glm() fits the same model with less code:

glm(sore_throat ~ treatment + bmi + smoking,
    family = binomial, data = sore) |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  term              estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>                <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 (Intercept)          1.02     0.979     0.0245 0.980       0.149     7.02 
2 treatmentlicorice    0.384    0.316    -3.02   0.00252     0.204     0.707
3 bmi                  0.950    0.0385   -1.34   0.179       0.879     1.02 
4 smokingpast          4.38     0.428     3.45   0.000551    1.94     10.5  
5 smokingcurrent       1.89     0.410     1.55   0.121       0.859     4.33 



family = binomial is what makes glm() a logistic regression
The same odds ratios and intervals as logistic_reg()
We use tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps

licorice_gargle from medicaldata, contributed by Amy Nowacki (TSHS Resources Portal)
Odds ratios with tidymodels follow the analysis and tidymodels chapters of Data Science for the Biomedical Sciences

t.test(Birthweight ~ Group, data = opt_clean, var.equal = TRUE)


    Two Sample t-test

data:  Birthweight by Group
t = 0.50991, df = 791, p-value = 0.6103

The t statistic has the same size as the regression’s (the sign flips because t.test() subtracts treatment from control), and the p-value is identical. A regression with one two-level predictor is a two-sample t-test with equal variances.

title: The class notes prompt
text:
This is all AI/Claude generated

We are building one prompt together that turns a class transcript into notes. You propose changes, we merge them, and all of the course’s notes get regenerated from the result — so an improvement you make after the lab also improves the notes for the lecture.



File
What it is




prompt-notes.md
The prompt. Every word of it is sent to the model, followed by a session’s transcript and slides. This is the file we edit together.


prompt-notes-<name>.md
Optional variants, for trying an idea next to the main prompt (see below).


README-prompt.md
This file: how it all works, and how to change it.


Makefile
Shortcuts for running the generator (make notes and the others below).





Each class session has a folder under sessions/, named by date — with a suffix such as -lecture or -lab when there were two classes that day:







File
What it is




plaud.md
share link to the recording


transcript-plaud.md
the transcript: machine-generated, lightly cleaned up by Plaud ← input


materials.md
the session’s slides from the course website: their text, the R code, and the output it printed, each heading linked to its slide ← input


notes-plaud.md
Plaud’s own AI notes — the baseline to beat


notes-class-main--<model>.md
what prompt-notes.md produced, and which model wrote it ← output



Reading notes-plaud.md and notes-class-main--<model>.md side by side is the point. Plaud’s notes come from a generic summariser that has never heard of this course. Ours know what the course is about, turn “see you Wednesday” into a real date, and keep the questions people asked.
The slides make a big difference. Speech is a bad way to record code: a microphone hears “percent greater percent” where the slide says %>%, and the arguments disappear. The instructor live-codes from the slides, so the prompt treats them as the authority on what was typed and what it printed, and links each piece of code back to its slide.
Notes come from more than one model: Claude (--claude-opus-…) and open-weights Qwen models run on the instructor’s own hardware (--qwen…), so you can compare them too.



Ordinary Git and GitHub practice. From a terminal:

Terminal
git switch -c prompt/your-change-here      # new branch
$EDITOR prompt-notes.md                    # make your edit
git add prompt-notes.md
git commit -m "Ask for a glossary of new functions"
git push -u origin prompt/your-change-here

Or on GitHub itself: open prompt-notes.md, click the pencil icon, make your edit, and choose Create a new branch for this commit and start a pull request.
In the pull request, say what problem the change fixes. The convincing version is a before/after on one session (see below), quoting the part that got better. A good change fixes something you can point at — a section that comes out thin, a date the notes got wrong, a kind of content the notes keep dropping. “Make it better” is not something we can evaluate.
To try a bigger idea next to the main prompt instead of in place of it, copy it to prompt-notes-<name>.md (say prompt-notes-glossary.md). Its notes come out as notes-class-glossary--<model>.md, beside the main ones, so the two can be compared.



The generator is class_notes.py, in the class-notes/scripts/ folder of the public chendaniely/skills repository. It needs Python 3 and, for Claude models, the Claude Code CLI, logged in once (claude, then /login). It runs on your Claude subscription: no API key is needed.

Terminal
git clone https://github.com/chendaniely/skills ~/git/skills      # once
cn=~/git/skills/class-notes/scripts/class_notes.py

python3 $cn generate --dry-run                                     # what would run
python3 $cn generate --only sessions/2026-11-02 --prompt glossary
python3 $cn generate --only sessions/2026-11-02 --force --model sonnet
python3 $cn payload --only sessions/2026-11-02 > message.txt

payload prints the exact message the model receives — the prompt, the transcript and the slides — so you can take a session to any other tool or model and do your own thing with it. No Claude subscription? Paste that message into GitHub Copilot Chat in your Codespace, or another assistant. The Makefile wraps the common runs (make notes, make notes-force); point it at your copy with CLASS_NOTES=~/git/skills/class-notes/scripts/class_notes.py.



There is one prompt file, not v1.md, v2.md, v3.md: git log -p prompt-notes.md shows every revision with its diff. Every generated notes file ends with a footer that records where it came from:
---

- prompt: prompt-notes.md @ a1b2c3d
- prompt-hash: 3f9c0e2b7a41
- model: claude-opus-5-5 (requested: opus)
- backend: claude
- inputs: transcript-plaud.md, materials.md
- generated: 2026-11-04
opus is an alias meaning “the latest Opus”, and what it points at changes over time; claude-opus-5-5 is the model that actually ran, which is why it is also in the filename. When the alias moves to a newer model, regenerated notes land in a new file next to the old one, so models can be compared too. inputs says whether the notes had the slides or only the transcript. prompt-hash is a fingerprint of the prompt’s words, so a commit that doesn’t change them (a rename, a revert) never makes old notes look out of date. A prompt shown as @ uncommitted was run before that version of it was committed; the prompt-hash still pins down its exact words.



These transcripts include your voices, and this repository is public on GitHub, so anyone can read them, and anyone with a session’s plaud.md link can play its recording. Students appear in the transcript as Speaker 1, Speaker 2, and so on. The prompt instructs the model to keep it that way and never to attach a name to a question. If you change the prompt, keep that rule.

title: Tidy Data, Wrangling, and First Modelling
text:
Date Time: 2026-11-02 13:00:00
Location: ECC 100 LT
Instructor: Daniel Chen


Session 1 introduced the foundational principles of data cleaning and manipulation in R using the tidyverse ecosystem. The instructor defined “tidy data” as a standardized format where each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value is a single cell. Students learned to identify common violations of these rules—such as column headers containing values, multiple variables packed into one column, and variables split across rows and columns—and practiced reshaping messy datasets into tidy formats using pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().
After establishing tidy data, the lecture covered core data wrangling operations with dplyr. The class practiced selecting columns, filtering rows, and creating new variables with mutate(), emphasizing the pipe operator (|>) for chaining steps cleanly without creating intermediate variables. The session then transitioned to exploratory data visualization with ggplot2, demonstrating how to map variables to geometric objects like scatter plots, histograms, and bar charts based on their data types.
Finally, the instructor provided a first look at statistical modelling, explaining how tidy data enables clear model specification. Using a linear regression example, the class learned to fit a model, interpret the slope coefficient as a rate of change, and use the tidymodels framework (recipe, workflow, fit) to standardize the modelling pipeline. The session concluded with a demonstration of GitHub Copilot in Codespaces, showing how agentic AI can edit code directly to streamline the workflow.






Tidy data: A consistent data structure that makes analysis, visualization, and modelling straightforward. Defined by three rules: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each value is a cell.
Column headers as values: When column names (e.g., income brackets, years, weeks) actually represent levels of a variable, the dataset violates tidy principles. Resolved by pivoting wide to long.
Multiple variables in one column: When a single cell or header contains embedded information (e.g., sp_m_014 for diagnosis, gender, and age). Resolved by splitting headers or using separate().
Variables in rows and columns: When multiple variables (e.g., tmax and tmin) are stacked in rows while other dimensions (e.g., days) are spread across columns. Requires both pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().





pivot_longer(): Converts wide-format data into long-format data. Useful when values are spread across column headers. Key arguments include cols (which columns to pivot), names_to (new column for headers), and values_to (new column for values).
pivot_wider(): Converts long-format data into wide-format data. Useful when variables are stacked in rows and need to become separate columns. Uses names_from and values_from.
names_prefix / names_transform: Arguments in pivot_longer() to strip text prefixes from column names and immediately convert types (e.g., as.integer) during the pivot, avoiding messy strings.
values_drop_na = TRUE: Drops missing values during pivoting to keep the resulting dataset cleaner and avoid empty rows.





select(): Chooses specific columns to retain. Can use exact names or helper functions like starts_with() or ends_with().
filter(): Subsets rows based on logical conditions (>, <, ==, !=, &, |). Returns only rows where the condition evaluates to TRUE.
mutate(): Adds new columns or modifies existing ones. Does not alter the original dataset; output must be assigned to a new variable or piped forward.
group_by(): Groups the dataset by a categorical variable so that subsequent functions apply calculations to each group independently.
summarize(): Computes a single summary value (e.g., mean(), max(), n()) for each group. Requires na.rm = TRUE when calculating means or sums with missing values.
|> (pipe operator): Passes the result of the expression on its left as the first argument to the function on its right. Enables linear, readable chaining of operations.





ggplot(): Initializes a plot by mapping the dataset and aesthetic variables (aes()), which link columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill).
geom_point(): Creates scatter plots for two continuous/quantitative variables.
geom_histogram(): Creates histograms for one continuous variable, binning the data to show distribution.
geom_bar(): Creates bar charts for categorical variables. Automatically counts occurrences (stat = "count").
geom_col(): Creates bar charts when the counts are already calculated in the data (stat = "identity"), requiring explicit y mapping.
labs(): Adds human-readable titles, axis labels, and legend titles to polish the figure.





Outcome variable types: Dictates the modelling approach. Continuous outcomes (numbers) use regression; categorical outcomes (groups/labels) use classification.
Model formula: Uses the tilde (~) to separate predictors from the outcome. The variable on the left is what you predict; variables on the right are inputs.
Linear regression: Fits a straight line (\(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)). The slope coefficient (β₁) represents the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in the predictor. Highly interpretable in clinical/medical contexts.
tidymodels workflow: Uses recipe() to define preprocessing, linear_reg()/logistic_reg() to define the model, and workflow() + fit() to train it. Standardizes the modelling pipeline.







# Pew survey: pivot wide income columns into long rows
pew_tidy <- pew |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -religion,
    names_to = "income",
    values_to = "frequency"
  )
# Billboard chart: pivot week columns, drop "wk" prefix, convert to integer
billboard_tidy <- billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(date = date.entered + (week - 1) * 7) |>
  select(year, artist, track, time, week, rank, date)
# WHO TB data: pivot all non-ID columns, split header on "_" into 3 new variables
who2 |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !(country:year),
    names_to = c("diagnosis", "gender", "age"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "count",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
# Weather data: pivot days to long, make dates, pivot temp types to wide
weather_tidy <- weather |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("d"),
    names_to = "day",
    names_prefix = "d",
    names_transform = list(day = as.integer),
    values_to = "temp",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = element,
    values_from = temp
  ) |>
  select(id, date, tmax, tmin) |>
  arrange(id, date)



# Chain select, mutate, filter using the pipe
penguins |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000) |>
  filter(flipper_len > 190) |>
  select(species, flipper_len, body_mass_kg)
# Group by species and calculate average body mass
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(avg_body_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE))
The pipe (|>) passes the output of the left side directly as the first argument to the function on the right. This allows you to read the code chronologically (“and then…”) and avoids cluttering the environment with intermediate data frames.



# Scatter plot of flipper length vs body mass
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

# Add colour by species and custom axis labels
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  )
ggplot2 uses a layering system. You map data to aesthetics inside aes(), then add geometric layers (geom_) with +. Colour and fill map categorical variables to visual distinctions.



# Specify recipe, model specification, and fit workflow
house_recipe <- recipe(price ~ sqft, data = Sacramento)

house_spec <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  set_mode("regression")

house_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(house_recipe) |>
  add_model(house_spec) |>
  fit(data = Sacramento)
# View the fitted model coefficients
tidy(house_fit)
The recipe() function defines the mathematical relationship (price ~ sqft). The workflow() combines preprocessing and model definition, and fit() trains it. The coefficient table shows an intercept of ~13,859 and a slope of ~138.5, meaning each additional square foot increases the predicted house price by $138.50.




Codespace restart times & monitor setup: The instructor spent the first few minutes troubleshooting Zoom screen sharing and realizing he was looking at the wrong monitor. He noted that if a Codespace times out or is accidentally closed, it takes several minutes to rebuild and install dependencies, so leaving it running is recommended.
Excel visual flags vs. computer parsing: A student asked how computers handle Excel cells formatted with colours to indicate status. The instructor explained that R and other data tools do not read cell background colours; visual flags must be explicitly converted into a new column to be analyzable.






Q: What is the practical difference between geom_bar() and geom_col()? A: geom_bar() automatically counts the occurrences of categories in a single column (stat = "count"). geom_col() assumes the counts are already calculated in the dataset and draws bars based on the provided y-values (stat = "identity"). Use geom_col() when you’ve already summarized your data.

A: Unlike web chat interfaces that just return text to copy-paste, the agent in the Codespace reads your actual project files and can edit them directly. You can ask it to “make a plot from the patients data” and it will generate and save the code in your script, which you then review and accept. title: Tidy Data, Wrangling, and First Modelling
text:
Session 1 introduced the foundational principles of data cleaning and manipulation in R using the tidyverse ecosystem. The instructor defined “tidy data” as a standardized format where each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each value is a single cell. Students learned to identify common violations of these rules—such as column headers containing values, multiple variables packed into one column, and variables split across rows and columns—and practiced reshaping messy datasets into tidy formats using pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().
After establishing tidy data, the lecture covered core data wrangling operations with dplyr. The class practiced selecting columns, filtering rows, and creating new variables with mutate(), emphasizing the pipe operator (|>) for chaining steps cleanly without creating intermediate variables. The session then transitioned to exploratory data visualization with ggplot2, demonstrating how to map variables to geometric objects like scatter plots, histograms, and bar charts based on their data types.
Finally, the instructor provided a first look at statistical modelling, explaining how tidy data enables clear model specification. Using a linear regression example, the class learned to fit a model, interpret the slope coefficient as a rate of change, and use the tidymodels framework (recipe, workflow, fit) to standardize the modelling pipeline. The session concluded with a demonstration of GitHub Copilot in Codespaces, showing how agentic AI can edit code directly to streamline the workflow.

title: Tidy Data, Wrangling, and First Modelling
text:
Tidy data: A consistent data structure that makes analysis, visualization, and modelling straightforward. Defined by three rules: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each value is a cell.
Column headers as values: When column names (e.g., income brackets, years, weeks) actually represent levels of a variable, the dataset violates tidy principles. Resolved by pivoting wide to long.
Multiple variables in one column: When a single cell or header contains embedded information (e.g., sp_m_014 for diagnosis, gender, and age). Resolved by splitting headers or using separate().
Variables in rows and columns: When multiple variables (e.g., tmax and tmin) are stacked in rows while other dimensions (e.g., days) are spread across columns. Requires both pivot_longer() and pivot_wider().





pivot_longer(): Converts wide-format data into long-format data. Useful when values are spread across column headers. Key arguments include cols (which columns to pivot), names_to (new column for headers), and values_to (new column for values).
pivot_wider(): Converts long-format data into wide-format data. Useful when variables are stacked in rows and need to become separate columns. Uses names_from and values_from.
names_prefix / names_transform: Arguments in pivot_longer() to strip text prefixes from column names and immediately convert types (e.g., as.integer) during the pivot, avoiding messy strings.
values_drop_na = TRUE: Drops missing values during pivoting to keep the resulting dataset cleaner and avoid empty rows.





select(): Chooses specific columns to retain. Can use exact names or helper functions like starts_with() or ends_with().
filter(): Subsets rows based on logical conditions (>, <, ==, !=, &, |). Returns only rows where the condition evaluates to TRUE.
mutate(): Adds new columns or modifies existing ones. Does not alter the original dataset; output must be assigned to a new variable or piped forward.
group_by(): Groups the dataset by a categorical variable so that subsequent functions apply calculations to each group independently.
summarize(): Computes a single summary value (e.g., mean(), max(), n()) for each group. Requires na.rm = TRUE when calculating means or sums with missing values.
|> (pipe operator): Passes the result of the expression on its left as the first argument to the function on its right. Enables linear, readable chaining of operations.





ggplot(): Initializes a plot by mapping the dataset and aesthetic variables (aes()), which link columns to visual properties (x, y, colour, fill).
geom_point(): Creates scatter plots for two continuous/quantitative variables.
geom_histogram(): Creates histograms for one continuous variable, binning the data to show distribution.
geom_bar(): Creates bar charts for categorical variables. Automatically counts occurrences (stat = "count").
geom_col(): Creates bar charts when the counts are already calculated in the data (stat = "identity"), requiring explicit y mapping.
labs(): Adds human-readable titles, axis labels, and legend titles to polish the figure.





Outcome variable types: Dictates the modelling approach. Continuous outcomes (numbers) use regression; categorical outcomes (groups/labels) use classification.
Model formula: Uses the tilde (~) to separate predictors from the outcome. The variable on the left is what you predict; variables on the right are inputs.
Linear regression: Fits a straight line (\(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\)). The slope coefficient (β₁) represents the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in the predictor. Highly interpretable in clinical/medical contexts.
tidymodels workflow: Uses recipe() to define preprocessing, linear_reg()/logistic_reg() to define the model, and workflow() + fit() to train it. Standardizes the modelling pipeline.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Summary
Daniel Chen introduced a course sequence on data processing in R, covering data cleaning and transformation, visualization, modeling, and communicating results. The lectures emphasized tidy data: how to identify and reshape messy datasets, preserve information in analysis-ready form, and use Tidyverse tools for data manipulation and visualization. They also introduced regression and classification, linear regression interpretation, and an optional GitHub Codespaces environment with an AI coding agent.

title: MEDI 504A: Biostatistics with Tidyverse
text:
Knowledge Points

1. Course structure, materials, and working environment

The course covers data cleaning and transformation, visualization, linear and logistic regression, and communicating results through reports. The instructor described the upcoming modeling material as planned for Thursday, November 5, and also referred to the next class as Wednesday, November 4, 2026; the schedule references were inconsistent.
Slides and related materials are available through the course website via Canvas. Students can read the slide content on the site or print it to PDF for annotation.
Suggested references include R for Data Science, material from UBC’s introductory data science course (DSI 100), and the instructor’s dissertation-based textbook for teaching data science to clinicians, which includes health-related datasets. The instructor recommended the 2014 tidy-data paper as a reference through section 4.
Students may use a GitHub Codespace to explore without installing or changing software on their own computers. The suggested setup is to create a GitHub account, sign up for the Student Pack, and start the Codespace from the course website’s Code option. Initial setup or a restart can take about 10 minutes. The Student Pack and Codespaces include free resources subject to usage limits.
The Codespace includes Copilot connected to an LLM and supports an agentic workflow: the agent can read files, write or edit code directly, and propose changes for the user to keep or reject. This can avoid copying code between tools, but generated changes must be reviewed; large edits can be difficult to manage. Do not put passwords or sensitive patient data in code or share identifiable records with an LLM. Generic code and column names can be used for visualization help without exposing row-level data.
The instructor presented AI tools as aids, not replacements for understanding and checking the work. Readable, maintainable code is preferable to dense code, including code generated by AI.



2. Tidy data: principles and diagnosing messy structures

Tidy data has three principles:

Each variable forms a column.
Each observation forms a row.
Each cell contains one value.

Data that has been collected or manually curated is not necessarily ready for analysis. A layout convenient for people to view may not preserve information or support reliable computer operations.
Hadley Wickham’s 2014 paper, Tidy Data, established the principles discussed in class. The instructor noted an earlier formulation concerning types and observational units, while emphasizing the one-value-per-cell principle in the lecture.
Useful signs that data may be messy include:

Column headers that encode values, such as years, income ranges, or weeks (WK1, WK2, etc.), rather than variable names.
A single column containing different kinds of measurements. For example, a count column mixing disease cases and population totals makes summaries such as means or maxima hard to interpret.
Column names that encode several variables, such as diagnosis, gender, and age in a name like m014.
Spreadsheet formatting—such as cell colors used to flag “good” or “bad”—that carries information not represented in the data itself. Such flags should be stored explicitly in a separate column.

Tidy data helps make filtering, grouping, calculations, and statistical summaries meaningful. The Tidyverse is a metapackage that loads several packages, including tidyr, which provides tools for tidying data.



3. Reshaping data with pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(), and separate()

pivot_longer() gathers multiple columns into a longer format, placing former column headers in a key column and their contents in a value column. It is useful when headers encode values, such as income brackets or weekly rankings.
pivot_wider() turns unique values in a category column into separate columns, filling them with values from another column. It can separate different measurement types, such as minimum and maximum temperature.
These operations are conceptually similar to arranging fields in an Excel pivot table. Which one—or whether both—is needed depends on the dataset and the intended analysis.
Patterned columns can be selected by position, excluded with !, or matched by prefixes and other patterns. For example, columns beginning with WK can be gathered, and the prefix can be removed to leave the week number.
After removing a text prefix, convert numeric-looking values to numeric types. Otherwise, values may sort alphabetically (1, 10, 11, 2) rather than numerically.
separate() or pivot_longer() can split compound names into distinct variables. When curating data, delimiters such as underscores or dashes provide “breadcrumbs” that make automated separation more reliable.
If multiple observations share the same identifiers, include another variable to distinguish their source or context, such as the observer. Otherwise, software may aggregate or average duplicate observations unintentionally.


Examples discussed

Pew Research religion and income data: Income ranges appear as column headers alongside religion names. Pivoting longer makes it easier to group by religion, calculate totals, and filter or compare frequencies.
Billboard rankings: Weekly columns such as WK1 through WK70+ can be reshaped into fields for song information, week, and ranking. A song can then occupy multiple rows—one per chart week—and be analyzed by week or artist. Missing weeks or rankings can be handled during the transformation.
WHO tuberculosis and census data: Headers may compress demographics or diagnosis details. Separating them into fields such as diagnosis, gender, age, and count makes demographic aggregation more direct.
Antarctic expedition measurements: Records by location and date can contain missing minimum or maximum temperature readings, which require explicit handling.




4. Data storage, formats, and missing values

Relational databases divide complex institutional data, such as hospital records, among specialized tables for patients, encounters, and procedures. Linking records with identifiers such as Patient ID avoids repeatedly storing the same demographic information.
CSV files are widely usable for data exchange and tutorials because they do not require proprietary software. Excel files are common in ad hoc workflows and can be read in R with packages such as readxl; enterprise systems generally use other data infrastructure.
Spreadsheet layouts that put time-series observations in columns can encounter software column limits. The lecture cited an NHS COVID-19 tracking failure in which daily counts arranged across columns exceeded a spreadsheet limit, leading to lost or overwritten data and disrupted predictive models.
In R, actual missing values are represented by NA, distinct from empty strings or special codes such as 99. is.na() returns logical values; because TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0, summing is.na(column) counts missing values, while summing !is.na(column) counts non-missing values.



5. Tidyverse data manipulation

select() chooses columns, while filter() chooses rows that satisfy conditions. Columns can be selected by name or pattern—for example, names beginning with bill, ending in _text, or within a range such as Q21 through Q47. Multiple selections can be combined.
filter() conditions can use comparisons and logical operators. Use == to test equality; a single = is used for assignment or naming arguments. ! negates a condition, and | represents logical OR. Conditions can also be combined to require multiple criteria.
mutate() creates or transforms columns. For example, body mass in grams can be converted to kilograms by dividing by 1,000. For recoding or type conversion, creating an intermediate column can make it easier to verify the result before dropping the original with select().
The base R pipe, |> (available from R 4.0), chains operations in sequence and can replace the Tidyverse pipe %>%. It supports readable, vertically arranged workflows such as mutating, filtering, and selecting in order.
group_by() partitions data by one or more variables, and summarize() calculates statistics for each group. Summary functions include mean(), median(), min(), max(), and n(); multiple summaries can be produced in one call.



6. Dates and the Palmer Penguins dataset

When day values are spread across patterned columns, use pivot_longer() to gather them, extract the day from the column name, remove prefixes, convert the day to an integer, and retain the corresponding measurement.
Separate minimum and maximum measurements into distinct columns when a combined value column would make averages or extrema ambiguous.
Combine year, month, and day into a proper date or timestamp before date arithmetic. Computers can then calculate intervals between dates; time zones also need appropriate handling.
The Palmer Penguins dataset was used as a practice example. It contains 344 observations and eight columns, including species, island, sex, year, bill and flipper measurements, and body mass.
A two-step transformation can be easier to read and debug than a compact nested operation. Small differences in computing time are generally less important than code that can be understood and checked.



7. Visualization with ggplot2

ggplot2 expects tidy data. The aes() function maps columns to plot properties such as the x-axis, y-axis, and color; plots are built by adding layers with +.
Suitable basic plots depend on variable types:

Two continuous variables: scatter plot with geom_point().
One continuous variable: histogram.
Categorical variables: bar chart, which may be stacked or dodged.

geom_bar() uses stat = "count" to count observations for a categorical variable. geom_col() uses stat = "identity" and requires precomputed y-values. Use geom_col() when a summary table already contains counts or frequencies.
Labels, themes, and other styling can be added as layers.



8. Modeling: prediction targets and linear regression

A model needs clearly identified columns for its target and inputs. Inputs may be called predictors, independent variables, or Xs; the target may be called the response, dependent variable, or Y. Data cleaning and column selection can occur at different stages, and data work is iterative.
The target’s type determines the general prediction task:

A numeric target calls for regression, such as predicting age, an albumin score, or house price.
A categorical target calls for classification, such as predicting survival, disease status, or disease stage. Binary outcomes are common introductory examples.

In an R formula, the tilde separates the target from predictors: the target is on the left, and input variables are on the right. Predictors do not all need to be numeric; for example, a categorical variable can help predict a numeric outcome.
Visualize relationships before modeling when practical. A scatter plot can show the relationship between two numeric variables, though a model can include more predictors than can be displayed in a simple plot.
Linear regression models numeric outcomes. Its formula relates to y = mx + b: the target is y, predictors correspond to x terms, and coefficients represent slopes, with an intercept term. With multiple predictors, the model includes a coefficient for each.
In the Sacramento housing example, a coefficient of 138.5 for square footage indicates an expected increase of $138.50 in house price per additional square foot. Linear and logistic regression are commonly used in biostatistics partly because their results can often be described in interpretable terms. Logistic regression for categorical outcomes was introduced as upcoming material.



9. Course logistics

A session break was called for 2:08 PM on November 2, 2026. The lecture was recorded, and the course site was expected to include an audio transcript and AI-generated summary.
The instructor noted classroom display and Zoom setup issues. He also described having gone to the wrong building after misreading an invitation; the recording does not establish the intended venue.

text:
Assignments and Practice

Review the course website, slides, and available references. For the tidy-data concepts, read the 2014 paper through section 4.
If using the optional cloud environment, create a GitHub account, sign up for the Student Pack, and start the course Codespace.
Practice tidying data by checking that variables are columns, observations are rows, and cells contain single values. Store status flags in explicit columns rather than only through formatting such as color.
Practice pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(), pattern-based column selection, and splitting compound headers with clear delimiters. Convert extracted numeric values to numeric types.
Clean and tidy the Ebola dataset in R using the discussed methods; this was scheduled for November 4, 2026.
Practice select() and filter() with the Palmer Penguins dataset or another dataset, and continue working with group_by() and summarize().
Convert date components to timestamps before date arithmetic. Use plots to explore relationships between numeric variables before fitting a model.
For a modeling task, identify the target and predictors and select the relevant columns. If trying the Codespaces coding agent, review proposed edits before accepting them and do not put passwords or sensitive data in code.
